extracted.intended_audience: editors and journalists (especially travel journalists and newsroom decision-makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for producing travel journalism that intersects with other newsworthy issues (climate, culture, geopolitics, development) while balancing commercial and editorial pressures. Includes commissioning, reporting technique, story-planning and verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional travel journalism (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel coverage that intersects with other newsworthy issues such as climate, community development, geopolitics and socio-cultural tensions; allows both the complex and aspirational aspects of travel to exist on the same page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight experiences where a tourist’s dollar benefits local people, offer alternatives to over‑touristed cities, or help readers understand the socio‑cultural backdrop of a place so they behave sensitively when there. Use intersectionality to move beyond top‑10 listicles and luxury glorification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand the genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Broaden the parameters of travel writing to intersect with science, culture and economics to lend depth to a beat often dismissed as 'fluff'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a good travel story like a strong feature: use strong scenes, a nut graph, solid interviewees and data. Encourage contributions from other sections (e.g., foreign correspondents, climate reporters) to add expertise and depth. Example: weaving science and conservation into a travel feature (e.g., commercialisation of bush tucker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission locally
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission local writers who bring cultural and historical understanding of a place, fresh ideas, and depth/diversity to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local voices can portray a country accurately without exoticising it (example: Sri‑Lankan writer producing jackfruit feature for BBC Travel). Balance this with the value of experienced globetrotters when appropriate. Anti‑pattern: relying only on visiting journalists who impose a colonial lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experienced globetrotters with rigorous underpinning
rubrics_metrics.description: There is value in experienced, globetrotting travel journalists, but their reporting should be underpinned by research, interviews and a rigorous fact‑checking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commissioning non‑local journalists, ensure deeper research and verification to avoid superficial or inaccurate portrayals. This criterion complements commissioning locally rather than replacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stack stories (multi-story strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a single trip produce multiple features: a quick service journalism piece first, followed by a longer intersectional story that requires more research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the first story a destination guide or new property opening to satisfy audiences, hosts and advertisers; use the breathing room this creates to later publish a researched intersectional piece. This balances commercial needs with deeper reporting and builds trust among readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage conflicts from hosted press trips
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that hosted press trips can complicate objectivity because hosts (airlines, destination boards) may also be advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate by producing separate service pieces and deeper investigative/feature pieces (stacking), maintaining editorial independence, and being transparent about hosting. Anti‑pattern: single, uncritical coverage that parrots host messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entice and educate (frame regenerative tourism appealingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entice travel junkies with unique curated experiences and educate armchair travellers by exploring destinations through an issue lens; reframe sustainable tourism as desirable luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make regenerative tourism sexy (e.g., 'redefine sustainable travel as the new chocolate cake'), spotlight immersive, non‑performative community interactions (example: Maori community experiences), surface unexpected angles (e.g., LGBTQ revolution in Bhutan) and curate practical guidance for readers on how to spend time and money responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑check and verify sustainability claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Before championing something as sustainable or regenerative, establish whether this is really the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborate with climate journalists to evaluate corporate claims, ask direct questions of providers, avoid brands that fudge answers, spotlight organisations that genuinely do it right. This helps prevent greenwashing and false sustainability claims in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address environmental and human impacts ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conscious of travel’s carbon footprint and human costs such as overtourism, cultural erosion and depletion of local supplies; incorporate these impacts into reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualise travel within climate and socio‑economic realities (e.g., share data like 8–10% of CO2 emissions from travel/tourism), discuss tradeoffs and how tourism dollars can be harnessed as a force for good. Anti‑pattern: glamourised travel copy that ignores local environmental or social harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise commercial and audience value of intersectional coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersectional travel journalism creates new advertising opportunities and can differentiate subscription publications and attract news‑avoidant readers seeking positive, utility‑driven features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trusted intersectional coverage to host native/regenerative campaigns with aligned brands (example: Red Sea Global + Skift campaign). Position such coverage as a way to retain reader trust and open sponsorship while maintaining editorial standards; aim to produce content that appeals commercially without compromising accuracy.
